CITY COUNCIL OF MONTEREY PARK

  320 W. NEWMARK AVENUE, MONTEREY PARK, CA 91754

  Wednesday
  December 18, 2024
  6:30 p.m.

  MISSION STATEMENT
  The mission of the City of Monterey Park is to provide excellent service, foster growth
  and opportunity, and create a joyous and collaborative environment.

  LAND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
  We would like to acknowledge that the land we inhabit today was once known as
  Tovangaar, the home of the Gabrieleño-Tongva people. We show our respect to the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, as well as all Indigenous people, past, present, and future,
  and honor their labor as original caretakers of this land. We commit to uplifting the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, invite you to acknowledge the history, and join us in caring
  for this land.

GENERAL INFORMATION
Documents related to an Agenda item are available to the public in the City Clerk’s Office located at 320
West Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754, during normal business hours and the City’s website
at http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/AgendaCenter/City-Council-17.

The public may watch the meeting live on the city’s cable channel MPKTV (AT&T U-verse, channel 99
or Charter Communications, channel 182) or by visiting the city’s website at
http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/133/City-Council-Meeting-Videos. Per the Americans with Disabilities
Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this meeting, please call City Hall at (626) 307-1359
for reasonable accommodation at least 24 hours before a meeting. Council Chambers are wheelchair
accessible.

PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
You may speak up to 5 minutes on an/each Agenda item. You may combine up to 2 minutes of time with
another person’s speaking. No person may speak more than a total of 10 minutes. The Mayor and City
Council may change the amount of time allowed for speakers. Written Communication will be accepted
up to 24 hours before the meeting via email to mpclerk@montereypark.ca.gov or by completing an online
form at www.montereypark.ca.gov/writtencomm.

While all comments are welcome, the Brown Act does not allow the City Council to take action on any
item not on the agenda. The Council may briefly respond to comments after Public Communications is
closed. Persons may, in addition to any other matter within the City Council's subject-matter jurisdiction,
comment on Agenda Items at this time. If you provide public comment on a specific Agenda item at this
time, however, you cannot later provide comments at the time the Agenda Item is considered.

 SUBJECT:  Compliance Review of Development Agreement No. 2261-AA dated
  October 6, 2021 regulating real property at 100-200 South Garfield
  Avenue (the “Project”)

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Receiving and filing this report (NOTE: any alterations to the project proposed by
  Rykadan 005, LLC must be processed in accordance with applicable law, i.e.,
  the City Council may not “approve” any changes requested by the developer);
  and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
These actions are exempt from additional review under the California Environmental
Quality Act (California Public Resources Code §§ 2100, et seq., “CEQA”) and CEQA
Guidelines (14 California Code of Regulations §§ 15000, et seq.) pursuant to CEQA
Guidelines § 15061(b)(3) the common sense exemption that CEQA applies only to
projects which have the potential for causing a significant effect on the environment
applies to the recommended action. It can be seen with certainty that there is no possibility
that the proposed action has a significant effect on the environment.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
On November 20, 2024, a representative from Rykadan 005, LLC (“Rykadan” or the
“Developer”) submitted documents to the City Council during public comment (“Developer
Comments”). A copy of that document is attached for reference. In sum, Developer seeks
to amend a Project that the City Council approved in 2021 via Development Agreement
No. 2261-AA (the “Development Agreement”).

Section 6.1 of the Development Agreement provides that the City may conduct annual
reviews of the Project after building permits are issued to determine whether the
Developer is acting in good-faith compliance with the Development Agreement. Condition
of Approval (“COA”) Nos. 3, 5, 8, and 136 provide authority for the City Council to review

  Page 7 of 431
 Staff Report
Page 2 of 9
December 18, 2024

the Project at any time. Based upon the Developer Comments, it seems prudent to
provide the City Council with a full overview the Project’s status.

BACKGROUND:

  Ø Pre-Rykadan

The Project is the latest rendition of development proposals for the property located at
100 to 200 South Garfield Avenue (the “Property”). The Property was originally quarried
for sand and gravel (before 1948) and then became a landfill owned by Operating
Industries, Inc. (“OII”) for municipal solid waste (until 1984). The Property was part of an
area identified for redevelopment as part of the now dissolved Monterey Park
Redevelopment Agency (“RDA”).

In 2006, the City approved the Towne Center project at the Property (“Towne Center”) as
proposed by Magnus Sunhill, LLC (Precise Plan 04-04; Conditional Use Permit 05-16;
and Tentative Map 04-07 per Resolution No. 02-06). The Towne Center project was a
mixed-use project consisting of approximately 71,366 square feet of retail space and
114,200 square feet of for-sale residential condominiums.

Thereafter, in 2013 the City Council approved a development agreement with Magnus
Sunhill for the Town Center project (DA-12-01). Among other things, the 2013
development agreement required Magnus Sunhill to commence construction of Towne
Center by May 1, 2013. Magnus Sunhill, however, filed for bankruptcy following disputes
with its investors. Court proceedings between 2015 and 2018 ultimately resulted in
Rykadan acquiring the Property. Rykadan filed documents with the City in 2019 to begin
processing a revised Towne Centre project.

  Ø The Rykadan Project

Work for processing the Project began in earnest only in 2021. In late March 2021, the
City received conceptual architectural plans; in May 2021, the City provided draft
conditions of approval for a six-story mixed use development; and in July 2021, a traffic
impact study was prepared. At Rykadan’s request (and expense), in May 2021, the City
retained a consultant team to expedite processing the Project (the “City Team”). Creation
of the City Team allowed the Project to be considered and approved by the City Council
on October 6, 2021 upon a 3-0-2 vote. This is the Project as approved by the City Council:

  “[C]onstruction of a 509,295 square foot residential/commercial facility on
  2.19 acres located at 114 E. Garvey Avenue. The facility will consist of
  approximately 151 residential units totaling approximately 170,000 square
  feet; 7,800 square feet of amenity and lobby space; 43,902 square feet of
  commercial land uses (e.g., retail and restaurant space); and 16,000 square
  feet for back of house, trash and other ancillary uses. Parking spaces (509)
  will be provided on three subterranean parking levels and two above-grade

  Page 8 of 431
 Staff Report
Page 3 of 9
December 18, 2024

  levels. The bedroom mix is initially planned to be 1 studio, 27 1-bedroom,
  95 2-bedroom and 28 2-bedroom plus den units (the “Residential Units”).
  The commercial portion of the site will include a retail food establishment
  use, which will operate similar to a food court or a farmers’ market. Individual
  vendors will lease spaces within this area, and the remainder of the space
  will be circulation for visitors/customers and for seating. Alcohol sales will
  be permitted by individual vendors. As shown on the Site Map, Level 1
  includes a food hall, restaurant, and retail spaces, residential lobbies, back
  of house operations and storage, patio seating, and a main plaza along
  Garfield Avenue. Level 2 includes a food hall, restaurant, and retail spaces,
  and a fitness center, and patio seating along Garvey Avenue. Levels 3
  through 6 include residential units as follows: 37 units on Level 3, 38 on
  Level 4, 38 on Level 5, and 38 on Level 6.”

COA Nos. 5, 8 and 136 for the Project ensure that this Project – not a different one –
obtain building permits:

  “5.  This approval is for the project as shown on the plans reviewed
  and approved by the Planning Agency and on file. Before the City issues
  a building permit, the applicant must submit plans, showing that the project
  substantially complies with the plans and conditions of approval on file with
  the Director. Any subsequent modification must be referred to the Director.
  The Director may, but is not required to, approve minor or technical
  modifications (including, without limitation, modifications to these
  conditions), or refer such requested modifications to the Planning
  Agency.” (Emphasis added).

  “8.  Before building permits are issued, the applicant must submit plans
  demonstrating substantial compliance with the plans and conditions
  of approval on file with the Director. Any subsequent modification to the
  project as approved, including the site plan, floor plan, elevations,
  landscaping and materials, must be referred to the Director to determine
  whether the Planning Agency should review the proposed
  modification.” (Emphasis added).

  “136. City will not issue any development permit, including for grading,
  except in conformance with an approved Final Development Plan. The size,
  shape, arrangement, use, and location of buildings, walkways, parking
  areas, drainage facilities, and landscaped areas must be developed in
  substantial conformity with the approved development plan marked
  City Council Hearing dated October 6, 2021. Substantial conformity must
  be determined by the Director.” (Emphasis added).

In 2022, the City expected Rykadan to commence work on the Project. Among other
things, Rykadan’s representatives asserted (in May 2022) that Rykadan was

  Page 9 of 431
 Staff Report
Page 4 of 9
December 18, 2024

  “operating full speed ahead to get plan check documents prepared. ETA
  from architect is August 2022. If the City can expedite their approval
  process, they will move quickly with construction start. They are
  contemplating submitting permit set for excavation and shoring as soon as
  June. If the city can approve those plans quickly, they would like to get
  excavation and shoring started by Aug/Sept. They have planned for the
  groundbreaking ceremony on Friday, July 29th, and would like to have a list
  of potential guests whom they can invite from the City. If the City can provide
  that to me with an email list, I can forward it to them. They will send out
  invites by end of June…. They have selected the GC, KCS West, whom
  they should be familiar with since they worked with them on the Courtyard
  Marriott project.”

Thereafter, on June 14, 2022, Rykadan’s representative invited the City Council to a
ground-breaking event scheduled for July 29, 2022 (even though it had not submitted any
grading or building plans to the City Team for review).

Yet, despite various efforts by the City Team to assist Rykadan in securing a building
permit – including granting various administrative approvals for changes in parking
configurations – the applicant failed to obtain a building permit by the end of 2022.

This date is significant: on January 1, 2023, new uniform codes (i.e., building codes,
plumbing codes, fire codes) became effective throughout California. Which meant that
Rykadan’s building plans needed to be completely overhauled to comply with these new
regulations. Recognizing the hardship that Rykadan might experience in making such
changes, the City Council delayed implementation of these new regulations until April 1,
2023 if applicants submitted complete building plans before December 31, 2022.
Rykadan failed to meet this deadline. The City Team still, however, offered to consider
the building plans filed if Ryakadan could secure a grading permit before April 1, 2023.
Rykadan failed to meet that deadline.

Even then, the City Manager exercised emergency powers to extend the deadline from
April 1, 2023 to May 1, 2023 so that Rykadan could obtain a building permit (see attached
Staff Report dated April 5, 2023). By April, however, it was evident based on conversation
with Rykadan representatives that Rykadan would not obtain permits.

  Ø Modifications to the Project

Starting in April 2023, Rykadan’s representatives began requesting changes to the
Project. This was summarized in an email dated April 22, 2023 where Rykadan’s
attorney stated that

  “my understanding is that there are certain parts of the project that have
  become unrealistic in light of our ever changing economy and the costs of

  Page 10 of 431
 Staff Report
Page 5 of 9
December 18, 2024

  construction. For example, second floor retail and restaurant uses are in
  decline throughout the Southland and subterranean parking has become
  prohibitively expensive. Rykadan, therefore, has asked its architect to
  explore minor changes … in hopes of revising the approved plan
  administratively.”

By email dated April 23, 2023, the City Attorney responded as follows:

  “[l]et me be very blunt on this: the changes contemplated by your client’s
  team and communicated to the City project manager are not “minor
  changes” as identified by the DA. They are significant alterations to the
  overall project that will require City Council approval. Along those lines, be
  aware that none of the three Council Members who approved this project
  are on the City Council any longer: Mr. Sornoso is deceased; Mr. Liang is
  off council; and Mr. Chan is also off council. Council Members Yiu and Lo –
  who both abstained on the vote – are on the council. Plus, three new council
  members who never saw this project.

  The City has bent over backward to accommodate this project including,
  without limitation, delaying the impact of the 2022 uniform codes and
  administratively approving changes to the parking (which the City – with a
  stretch – considered to be a minor change as it did not affect the aesthetics
  of the overall project). Indeed, the City Manager was willing to exercise his
  emergency powers to further delay the imposition of the uniform codes until
  May 1st if your client had filed applications for off site improvements and
  grading. That did not occur notwithstanding the City’s project manager
  trying his best to get an application.

  Accordingly, whatever your clients are planning to do, it is more than likely
  that all plans will be subject to the 2022 uniform codes. The City’s project
  manager previously communicated this to your client’s team…. I do not see
  any need for a zoom meeting or reviewing architectural plans at this stage.
  Just submit what is desirable and we will process it with the City
  Council.” (Emphasis added).

The City Team suspended processing the Project on May 3, 2023, and the Project lay
dormant until May 2024 when Rykadan filed an application for “Project Entitlement
Modifications.”

By letter dated June 13, 2024, the City Team informed Rykadan (among other things)
that

  “[t]he proposed Celadon project in Monterey Park is substantially different
  in scale and residential density from the previously analyzed Towne Center

  Page 11 of 431
 Staff Report
Page 6 of 9
December 18, 2024

  project. The difference is going to require that certain additional analyses
  be performed.”

Apparently uncertain regarding why the City Team referred to the 2006 Towne Center
project (and after a meeting between the City Team and Rykadan representatives on
July 30, 2024), Rykadan’s attorney submitted a letter on August 6, 2024. Among other
things, the letter states that

  “Conditions of Approval nos. 5, 6, and 8 acknowledge that subsequent
  modifications to the Project may occur and are subject to approval by the
  Director or Planning Agency. Condition 8 even includes modifications to the
  site plan, floor plan, elevations, landscaping and materials within the ambit
  of such subsequent modifications. Condition nos. 134- 138 specifically refer
  to the preliminary and final development plans, including any "revised plans"
  and "any changes to the size, colors, construction materials, design or
  location of any structure on site, or other site or landscape improvements"
  being made simply with the approval of the Director. All the proposed
  revisions are changes to the size, colors, design, location of the
  structures on site, etc., and thus fall within the ambit of these
  provisions of the DA.” (Emphasis added).

The emphasized language, however, omitted the provisions of the COA stating that the
Director may refer substantial revisions of the Project to the Planning Agency (i.e., the
City Council) in the Director’s discretion (see above). To remove any doubt, the City
Attorney responded to Rykadan’s attorney on the same date (August 6th). After
repeating the communication from April 23, 2023, regarding the proposed Project
amendments, the City Attorney stated

  “[l]et me cut to the chase: if your client wants these substantial modifications
  approved and building permits issued, it will take a trip to the City Council.
  My suggestion is that this be sped up so that we are not (again) left
  wondering what your client is doing.”

On October 10, 2024, the City Team met in person with Rykadan’s Project manager and
several new Rykadan’s representatives. There was no change in the messaging.
Rykadan’s representatives were informed that the proposed changes were substantial;
would require City Council approval; and would require environmental review. As to the
latter, the extent of review was uncertain until Rykadan’s application included more than
conceptual drawings. Rykadan’s representatives were encouraged to file an application
so that the City could determine next steps. Rykadan’s November 20, 2024,
communication with the City Council followed. It does nothing to assist with the City
Team’s ability to process revisions to the Project.

  •  CEQA Challenges

  Page 12 of 431
 Staff Report
Page 7 of 9
December 18, 2024

At the applicant’s request, the Project was approved in 2021 based upon a Class 32
Categorical Exemption. This type of categorical exemption requires that a project align
with the General plan and zoning regulations; be located on a site not larger than five
acres surrounded by urban uses; and have no significant habitat value for endangered
species. Additionally, the project must not cause significant impacts on traffic, noise, air
quality, or water quality, and the site must be adequately serviced by necessary utilities
and public services. The City Council made those findings in 2021.

A revision to the Project requires environmental review. This will pose challenges for
various reasons. Most significantly is that the 2006 Towne Center project utilized a
mitigated negative declaration (“MND”) that used data from the 2000 Final Environmental
Impact Report (“2000 FEIR”) certified for updates to the City’s General Plan. While a draft
Addendum to the 2006 MND was prepared for the Project in 2021 (authored by CAJA
Environmental Services), it was not approved by the City Council because the applicant
wished to accelerate the timeline for the City’s decision-making. The time for challenging
the environmental decisions for the Project are long expired. Changes in California law –
and the City’s General Plan (including, e.g., the Housing Element) – since 2000, however,
will require greater scrutiny of any proposed amendments to the Project.

The Project utilized data and assumptions from the 2006 Towne Center MND (and the
draft 2021 Addendum) to support findings needed to fit the Project into a Class 32
exemption. Some of those data and assumptions are now more than 20 years old. CEQA
requires that data be “current.” Most agencies utilize a five-year guideline to ensure that
there is a fresh look at potential impacts and mitigation measures, i.e., environmental data
older than five years may require updating. Examples:

  •  The Project’s need to comply with stormwater regulations (Low Impact
  Development or “LID” plan and report) in 2021 was to be accomplished by paying
  an in-lieu fee to allow for an offsite project. That option, however, is no longer
  available as the regulations changed in late 2021.

  •  The traffic surveys conducted for the Project in 2020 are now stale and will need
  to be either redone or (at a minimum) peer reviewed considering changes to traffic
  regulations.

  •  Traffic signal improvements associated with the project impacts will now require
  re-evaluation for adequacy and likely different traffic signal improvements may be
  warranted based on the current state of signalized intersection improvements the
  City has been implementing over the past three years.

  •  Because the 2021 agreements with the LA County Sanitation District regarding
  wastewater connection quantity and connection fees are outdated, those
  agreements related to the project need to be re-evaluated and confirmed.

  •  Fire Department access requirements that were previously exempted from the
  project will now require review under the current Fire Department requirements,

  •  Southern California Edison infrastructure improvements were proposed for the
  Project in 2021. The status of those power improvements is uncertain, but that will

  •  While the Project identified measures to reduce the impact of noise and vibration
  upon neighboring properties – including the Lincoln Plaza Hotel – considering

  Ø Challenges to processing Project Amendments

Rykadan was registered in California in 2014 and acquired the Property in 2018. Its parent
company is Rykadan Capital, Ltd. which incorporated in the Cayman Islands in 2009.
Public reports show that Rykadan Capital has a net worth of $131,243,257 in the United
States.

Based upon public documents, the Project in Monterey Park is Rykadan’s biggest – and
most complex – development project. It is more than twice the size of the next biggest
project located in Hong Kong (the Wong Chuk Hang Project of 107,208 square feet).
Rykadan is involved with much smaller projects (e.g., single family residential) in the
United States (in San Marino, Arcadia, and San Gabriel).

Between 2019 and 2021, Rykadan utilized a team of well-seasoned individuals who were
familiar with California’s (and the City’s) regulatory requirements for the Project. Since
then, however, those individuals are no longer part of Rykadan’s team. These changes
may have contributed to the overall inability for the Project to secure permits in 2022 and
its challenges since that date.

  Ø Conclusion

As recommended, this Staff Report is a receive and file item intended to update the City
Council regarding Rykadan’s compliance with the Project approvals. Should Rykadan
complete its application for changes, the City Team will process it in accordance with
applicable law and present it to the City Council for consideration. The application will
not be approved administratively.

  without limitation, extending the effective date for issuing building permits for the

  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

On January 8, 2023 (as ratified by Resolution No. 2023-R5, adopted January 18, 2023)
and, separately, on January 31, 2023 (Resolution No. 2023-R7), the City declared local
emergencies. The first local emergency was in response to the 2023 Winter Storms that
continue to stretch the City’s resources; the second was in response to the Mass Casualty
Incident resulting in the death of 11 people on January 21, 2023 (collectively, the “2023
Emergencies”).

The City Manager, acting in his capacity as the Emergency Services Director, undertook
various actions to prioritize the use of public resources to manage the 2023 Emergencies.
Among other things, public safety and public works personnel were mobilized in response
to visits by the President and Vice-President of the United States; the Governor of
California; and multiple, additional, dignitaries.

This report is submitted to the City Council in compliance with Government Code § 8630.
It also requests that the City Council ratify several actions taken by the City Manager in
accordance with his emergency powers under the 2023 Emergencies and that the 2023
Emergencies by extended to May 1, 2023.

BACKGROUND:

A consequence of responding to the 2023 Emergencies is that the City’s resources are
stretched thin. While the Police and Fire Departments were the most affected, the Public
Works Department – which responds to storm damage, infrastructure needs, and street
closures (for example, in response to POTUS’s visit) – is also significantly affected.
Among other things, the 2023 Emergencies interfered with the Public Works
Department’s ability to process building plans for various pending projects that were
approved by the City Council in 2022.

On January 1, 2023, various uniform codes imposed by the State of California became
effective. Ordinance No. 2224 (adopted November 16, 2022) implements the uniform
codes within the City of Monterey Park. Section 23 of Ordinance No. 2224 provides

  “[p]rojects for which a building permit application and building plans were
  submitted before the effective date of this Ordinance, and for which building
  permits are obtained within 90 days from the effective date … are exempt
  from the regulations in the 2022 [uniform] code update including the
  [uniform] codes adopted by reference….”

The Celadon project was approved by the City Council in 2021 via Ordinance No. 2215
(adopted October 20, 2021). Among other things, Ordinance No. 2215 approved a
development agreement (“DA”) between the City and Rykadan. Section 4.2 of the DA
provides, in part, that the City “will not unreasonably withhold … any [permits] that may
be issued by City in order for the [Celadon] Project to proceed….” Although the DA
contains a specific exemption from this general requirement for the uniform codes
adopted by Ordinance No. 2224, the 2023 Emergencies also activated Section 10.22 of
the DA which is captioned “Unavoidable Delays or Events.” Among other things, that
section provides that the time for performing under the DA will be excused during a delay
caused by “terrorism … floods … governmental restrictions … or similar bases….”

Rykadan filed all processing fees and paperwork in 2022 to secure a building permit
before April 1, 2023 (the deadline established by Ordinance No. 2224). The 2023
Emergencies, however, delayed the City’s review (and response to corrections) by at
least three weeks. Indeed, the Police Department is just now conducting its initial review
of the Rykadan plans; the Fire Department is undergoing its second review of the plans.
Overall, the City’s project manager for Celadon estimates that building permits may be
issued by May 1, 2023. Based upon the foregoing, the City Manager utilized his
emergency powers to extend the deadline for Celadon obtaining a building permit from
April 1, 2023 to May 1, 2023. The City Council is asked to ratify this action.

Permits for other Celadon project related work are being issued before the April 1st
deadline established by Ordinance No. 2224: grading and demolition permits are being
issued to allow Rykadan to proceed with offsite SCE undergrounding work; offsite curb,

  The City Council of the City of Monterey Park does ordain as follows:

SECTION 1: The City Council finds and declares that:

  General Plan and Zoning Map when they adopted the Land Use and Urban Design
  Element of the General Plan (“LUE”);

B.  This Ordinance changes the zoning designation for several properties to conform
  to the adopted LUE;

C.  This Ordinance was reviewed by the City Planner for, in part, consistency with
  the General Plan, and conformity with the Monterey Park Municipal Code
  (“MPMC”);

D.  In addition, the City reviewed the environmental impacts of this Ordinance under
  the California Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et
  seq., (“CEQA”) and the regulations promulgated thereunder (14 California Code
  Regulations §§ 15000, et seq., the “CEQA Guidelines”);

E.  The City Planner completed its review and scheduled a public hearing regarding
  this Ordinance before the City Council for December 4, 2024;

F.  Notice of the Public Hearing before the City Council was duly given and
  published in the time, form, and manner as required by law;

G.  On December 4, 2024, the City Council held a public hearing to receive public
  testimony and other evidence regarding the proposed re-zoning including, without
  limitation, information provided to the City Council by the City Planner and public
  testimony; and

H.  The findings in this Ordinance are made based on the entire administrative record
  including testimony and evidence presented the City Council at its December 4,
  2024, public hearing including, without limitation, the staff report submitted by the
  City Planner.

SECTION 2: Factual Findings and Conclusions. The City Council finds as follows:

SECTION 3: Environmental Assessment. The City Council reviewed the environmental
impacts of this proposed Ordinance pursuant to the California Environmental Quality Act
(Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq. “CEQA”) and the regulations promulgated
thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regs. §§ 15000, et seq., the “CEQA Guidelines”). CEQA
Guidelines § 15168 provides that a Program EIR may be prepared to consider the
environmental impacts of a series of actions that can be characterized as one large
project that are related as logical parts in a chain of contemplated actions. The City
Council finds as follows:

A.  On December 5, 2019, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 12126 approving
  a Focused General Plan update to the City’s LUE and Final Environmental Impact
  Report (“FEIR”) (SCH No. 2001-01-1074).

B.  The FEIR is a Program EIR that evaluated the environmental impacts resulting
  from the LUE implementation which is attached as Exhibit B and incorporated by
  reference.

C.  Changing the zoning designation for those properties identified in this Ordinance
  is an activity contemplated by the LUE and analyzed under the FEIR.

D.  This Ordinance does not contemplate any changes which will require major
  revisions to the FEIR nor are there any substantial changes with respect to the
  circumstances under which the FEIR was undertaken.

E.  There is no new information of substantial importance, which was not known and
  could not have been known with the exercise of reasonable diligence at the time
  the FEIR was certified showing: (1) the zone change will have one or more
  significant effects not discussed in the FEIR; (2) significant effects previously
  examined will be substantially more severe than shown in the FEIR; (3) mitigation
  measures or alternatives previously found not to be feasible would in fact be
  feasible and would substantially reduce one or more significant effects of the
  project; or (4) mitigation measures or alternatives which are considerably different
  from those analyzed in the FEIR would substantially reduce one or more significant
  effects on the environment.

SECTION 4: Zone Change Findings. Pursuant to MPMC §§ 21.38.050 and 21.42.010,

  Page 65 of 431
 ORDINANCE NO.
PAGE 3 OF 13

the City Council finds as follows:

A.  The zone change is consistent with the goals, policies and objectives of the
  General Plan and will create consistency between the LUE designations and zone
  designations on the Zoning Map. The zone change affects areas that have a voter
  approved Land Use designation that implements the LUE (Measure JJ). The
  correlations between the proposed zone changes and General Plan Land Use
  designations exist as follows:

  (1)  The Monterey Park LUE identifies Innovation/Technology designation as an
  area for primary uses related to research and development, light
  manufacturing, service commercials, professional offices, entertainment,
  and breweries/wineries/distilleries. The LUE also identifies retail and service
  commercial uses as support services within the Innovation/Technology
  designation.

  (2)  LUE Policy 24.1 seeks to ensure that zoning regulations applicable to the
  Monterey Pass Road corridor permit the range of uses necessary to achieve
  land use goals and prohibit uses that conflict with those goals.

  (3)  The O-P – Office Professional zone provides for the development of
  integrated professional, office and limited retail areas that exhibit a diversity
  of business activity.

  (4)  The LUE Land Use Plan identifies the Commercial designation as an area
  for primary uses related to a broad range of retail and service commercial
  uses, hospitality, entertainment, medical, and professional office. The LUE
  also identity uses such as schools, public assembly uses, public utilities,
  community care facilities and similar within the Commercial designation.

  (5)  LUE Policy 11.1 seeks to ensure that new commercial developments
  address privacy issues relative to any abutting residential neighborhoods,
  to ensure adequate transition and compatibility between commercial and
  residential uses.

  (6)  The C-P – Commercial-Professional zone provides for the development of
  commercial areas that promote retail and provide transition areas between
  the City and neighboring communities.

  (7)  The C-S – Commercial Services zone provides for the development of
  commercial areas that promote retail and provide transition areas between
  the City and neighboring communities.

  (8)  The LUE Land Use Plan identifies the Open Space designation as an area
  for parks and City-Owned recreational facilities, community gardens, golf
  course, and resource conservation areas. The LUE also identity public utility

  Page 66 of 431
 ORDINANCE NO.
PAGE 4 OF 13

  facilities and historic landfills as uses within the Open Space designation.

  (9)  The O-S – Open Space zone provides for the establishment and provision
  of permanent outdoor recreational and open space resources, and to
  prevent inappropriate development of areas which should be regulated to
  provide for recreational, conservation, aesthetic, historic, cultural, scenic or
  public health and safety uses.

  (10)  The LUE Land Use Plan identifies the Medium Density designation as an
  area for primary uses that include attached or detached residential units,
  with private common open space, at densities ranging from 8.1 – 16.0 units
  per acre.

  (11)  The R-2 – Medium Density Residential zone provides medium density
  residential housing either attached or detached multiple-family units at a
  density of 16 units per acre.

  (12)  The Monterey Park Land Use and Urban Design Element identifies High
  Density designation as an area for primary uses that include attached or
  detached residential units, with private common open space, at densities
  ranging from 16.1 to 30 units per acre.

  (13)  The R-3 – High Density Residential zone provides high density residential
  housing either attached or detached multiple-family units at a density of 30
  units per acre.

B.  The zone change will not adversely affect surrounding properties. This Ordinance
  is an administrative action that does not contemplate any development or
  otherwise impact any property other than the specific properties being rezoned,
  which will bring consistency to and is part of the City’s broader land use efforts as
  reflected in the adopted LUE.

C.  The proposed zone change promotes public health, safety, and general welfare
  and serves the goals and purposes of the MPMC’s zoning regulations since it will
  harmonize the General Plan LUE designations and the MPMC. Additionally, this
  activity is consistent with the various goals an policies of the LUE as identified in
  this Ordinance.

 SUBJECT:  A public hearing to consider introduction and first reading of Zone
  Change No. ZC-24-03 (“ZC-24-03”), an Ordinance to rezone certain
  properties within the City to be consistent with the General Plan Land
  Use and Urban Design Element.

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Opening a public hearing and taking testimonial and documentary evidence;
  2. After closing the public hearing and considering the evidence submitted during that
  public hearing, introducing and waiving first reading of Ordinance No. _____
  amending the zoning map for certain properties for consistency with the General
  Plan, Land Use and Urban Design Element; and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
The City reviewed the environmental impacts of the proposed Ordinance pursuant to the
California Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq. “CEQA”)
and the regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regs. §§ 15000, et seq.,
the “CEQA Guidelines”). CEQA Guideline § 15168 provides that a Program EIR may be
prepared to consider the environmental impacts of a series of actions that can be
characterized as one large project that are related as logical parts in a chain of
contemplated actions. The proposed Ordinance is within the scope of the City’s Focused
General Plan Update to the Land Use and Urban Design Element which was evaluated
under a Final Environmental Impact Report (“FEIR”) (SCH No. 2001-01-1074). The FEIR
adequately describes and considers the proposed Ordinance for CEQA purposes.
Accordingly, the Ordinance is not subject to further environmental review.

TYPE OF ACTION (LEGISLATIVE)
In considering the Zone Change, the City Council acts in its discretionary legislative
capacity. The City Council must make the following findings pursuant to MPMC section
21.38.050:

  •  That the proposed amendment is consistent with the goals, policies, and
  objectives of the General Plan;

  •  That the proposed amendment will not adversely affect surrounding properties;
  and
  •  That the proposed amendment promotes public health, safety, and general
  welfare and serves the goals and purposes of the Zoning Code.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
On November 3, 2020, the City’s voters initiated changes to the zoning designations for
properties throughout the City for consistency between the General Plan and Zoning Map
when they voted to approve the Land Use and Urban Design Element of the General Plan
(“LUE”).

In 2023, the City began efforts in the Our City, Our Plan Campaign to implement the
General Plan Land Use and Urban Design Element (“LUE”) and the Housing Element
(“HE”), which sets the vision for development within the City. The General Plan is
implemented through the zoning regulations located in Title 21 of the Monterey Park
Municipal Code (“MPMC”). MPMC section 21.02.220 adopts a zoning map which assigns
a zoning designation to each property in the City. This proposed ordinance will change
the zoning designations for properties throughout the City to harmonize the zoning
designation with the General Plan Land Use Designation consistent with voter’s approval
of the LUE.

BACKGROUND:
The LUE was voter approved by Measure JJ in November of 2020. The HE was approved
by the City Council in November 2022, and certified by the California State Department
of Housing and Community Development (“HCD”) in March 2023. As part of the work to
implement the LUE and HE, the Community Development Director is proposing to re-
zone certain properties listed in the proposed Ordinance (Attachment 2) to bring
consistency between the General Plan and the MPMC.

ANAYLSIS
If adopted, the Ordinance will make the Zoning Map consistent with the General Plan land
use designation as established in Figure LU-3, Land Use Policy Map (Attachment 1) in
compliance with State law (Government Code § 65860). ZC-24-03 will impact specific
properties across the City, where their zoning designation is inconsistent with adopted
land use designations. The affected land use designations and zoning districts are listed
in the table below:

 SUBJECT:  Acceptance of SGVMWD Grant for Irrigation Control Systems

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Accepting and allocating grant funding in the amount of $50,000 from the San
  Gabriel Valley Municipal Water District (“SGVMWD”) for Irrigation Control
  Systems;
  2. Authorizing the City Manager to execute the Grant Agreement, in a form approved
  by the City Attorney, with SGVMWD for this grant program;
  3. Authorizing the Finance Department to appropriate $50,000 in funding from the FY
  2024-2025 budget; and
  4. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The San Gabriel Valley Municipal Water District (“SGVMWD”) is awarding the city
$50,000 grant funding for water conservation projects. The grant requires that the City
first spend its funds, and submit invoices to SGVMWD for reimbursement. The Public
Works Director (“Director”) requests the City Council allocate $50,000 from the FY 2024-
2025 budget (“Budget”), and accept grant funding from SGVMWD reimbursing the City in
the same amount and allocate such grant funding to the Budget.

BACKGROUND:
The SGVMWD is offering each of its four member cities (Alhambra, Azusa, Monterey
Park, and Sierra Madre) $50,000 in grant funding. SGVMWD approved the City’s
proposal to use these funds for smart irrigation control systems. These systems include
an array of sensors that monitor water flow, evapotranspiration, rain, wind and soil
moisture and provides real-time onsite data to the controllers. The software then analyzes
the data to ensure that the irrigation system makes the most efficient use of water.

The grant will be disbursed to the City upon receipt of invoices from the City for
implementing the program. The maximum grant amount is $50,000.

The Director is requesting that City Council accept SGVMWD’s $50,000 grant to purchase
smart irrigation control systems and allocate the grant funds in the Budget.

The following requirements are added to establish storm water and urban runoff pollution
prevention controls.

Storm or construction generated water containing sediment such as, construction waste,

transit mixers or other pollutants from construction sites and parking areas will be
retained or controlled on site and will not be permitted to enter the storm drain system.

Temporary sediment filtering systems such as sandbags, silt fences, or gravel berms
will be utilized to trap sediment so that only filtered water enters the City’s storm drain
system. Proper clean up and disposal of settled sediment and the filtering system will be
the responsibility of the Contractor.

Discharge of concrete transit mixer wash water on to approved dirt areas (sub-grade area
designated for new concrete construction for example) is acceptable. Discharge on to
private property, parkway areas, or the street is not permitted.

Plastic or other impervious covering will be installed where appropriate to prevent
erosion of an otherwise unprotected area, along with any other runoff control devices
deemed appropriate by the City.

Excavated soil stored on the site will be covered in a manner that minimizes the amount
of sediments running into the storm drain system, street or adjoining properties.

No washing of construction or other industrial vehicles and equipment will be allowed
adjacent to a construction site. During the rainy season (October 15 to April 15),
Contractor will keep at the construction site sufficient materials and labor to install
temporary sediment filtering systems and other water pollution prevention control

STREET CLASSIFICATIONS

Each of these segments is classified and defined with roadway classifications as listed in the
California Road Systems (CRS) Maps that are approved by the Federal Highway Administration
and maintained by the Department of Transportation (CVC 40802). Functional classifications are
used in determining which type of roads are eligible for Federal funding to maintain the roads.
Usually Principal Arterials, Secondary Arterial and Major Collectors are eligible.

Functional classification is the process by which streets and highways are grouped into classes, or
systems, according to the character of service they are intended to provide. Basic to this process
is the recognition that individual roads and streets do not serve travel independently in any major
way. Rather, most travel involves movement through a network of roads. Functional classification
defines how a particular road or street plays in serving the flow of trips through a highway network.
The four functional systems for urbanized areas are urban principal arterials, minor arterials, major
collectors, and local roads.

Principal Arterial: Principal Arterials carry most of the trips entering and leaving the City as well as
serves the major centers of activity of a City, carries the highest traffic volume along its corridors
while carrying the major portion of trips entering and leaving the urban area.

Secondary Arterial: The secondary arterial street system includes all arterials not classified as
principal and contains facilities that place more emphasis on land access than the higher system

and offer a lower level of traffic mobility. Such facilities may carry local bus routes and provide
intra-community continuity, but ideally should not penetrate identifiable neighborhoods. This
system should include urban connections to rural collector roads where such connections have
not been classified as urban principal arterials.

Collector: The collector street system provides both land access service and traffic circulation
within residential neighborhoods, commercial and industrial areas. It differs from the arterial system
in that facilities on the collector system may penetrate residential neighborhoods, distributing trips
from the arterials through the area to the ultimate destination. Conversely, the collector street also
collects traffic from local streets in residential neighborhoods and channels it into the arterial
system.

Local: These roadways provide direct access to individual residential properties, schools, and
churches typically with a posted speed of 25 MPH. Through traffic on local streets are usually
discouraged. Local roads within residential and business district zones are not subject to Speed
Trap provisions and are posted at the Prima Facie speed limit. Service to through traffic movement
is usually deliberately discouraged.

CALIFORNIA VEHICLE CODE:

Speed limits in California are governed by the California Vehicle Code (CVC), Sections 22348
through 22413. The statutes establish or provide means of establishing speed limits by:

1. Basic speed limit law.
  Section 22350 of the CVC provides that no person shall drive a vehicle upon a highway at a
  speed greater than is reasonable or prudent having due regard for weather, visibility, traffic
  and the surface and width of the highway, and in no event at a speed which endangers the
  safety of persons or property. This is the basic speed limit law.

2. Prima facie speed limits are specified by statute or established by the State or local authorities
  within their respective jurisdictions on the basis of an engineering and traffic survey. Prima facie
  speed limits are specific limits stated in the CVC or specific limits established on the basis of an
  engineering and traffic survey authorized by the CVC. Prima facie speed limits are preempted
  by the basic speed limit law when the conditions in CVC Section 22350 are met.

  Section 22352 of the CVC establishes prima facie speed limits as follows and shall be
  applicable unless changed as authorized in the CVC and if so changed, only when signs have
  been erected giving notice of the change:

  a. Fifteen miles per hour.
  • At a railroad grade crossing with an obstructed view.
  • At an uncontrolled highway intersection with an obstructed view.
  • In an alley.

  b. Twenty-five miles per hour.
  • On any highway other than a State highway, in any business or residence district, CVC
  Sections 235 and 515 define a "business district” and a “residence district” respectively.
  Section 240 and 40802 of the CVC prescribes a method for determining whether a
  highway can be considered within a business or residence district.
  • Unless a different limit is established by procedures described elsewhere in the code.
  • In a school zone, posted with SCHOOL warning signs.
  • When passing a facility primarily used by senior citizens and contiguous to a street other
  than a State highway and posted with a SENIOR warning sign.

LOCAL AUTHORITY TO ESTABLISH PRIMA FACIE SPEED LIMITS:

Sections 22357 and 22358 of CVC authorize local authorities to establish prima facie speed limits
on streets and roads under their jurisdiction on the basis of an engineering and traffic survey. The
declared prima Facie limits shall become effective when appropriate signs giving notice are
erected upon the street.

SPEED TRAP:

Section 40802 2B(i) of the CVC provides that prima facie speed limits established under Sections
22352, 22354, 22357, 22358 and 22358.3 may not be enforced by radar unless the speed limit has
been justified by an engineering and traffic survey conducted within one of the following time
periods; five years to the date of the violation, within the last 7 years or if an engineering and traffic
survey was conducted more than 7 years prior to the date of the alleged violation, and a
registered engineer evaluates the section of the highway and determines that no significant
changes in roadway or traffic conditions have occurred, including, but not limited to, changes in
adjoining property or land use, roadway width, or traffic volume, the survey applies for 14 years.

This section does not apply to local streets, roads, school zones or senior zones which have been
set at the Prima Facie speed limit. Local streets are defined to have the following characteristics:
  • Width not more than 40 feet
  • Not more than .5 miles of uninterrupted length
  • 1 lane in each direction

primarily used by senior citizens or the grounds thereof that is posted with a standard “Senior”
warning sign pursuant to Section 22352.

ENGINEERING AND TRAFFIC SURVEY:

Section 627 of CVC defines the term engineering and traffic survey and lists its requirements.
Section 627 states: "An engineering and traffic survey shall include, among other requirements
deemed necessary by the Department of Transportation, consideration of all of the following:
prevailing speeds as determined by traffic engineering measurements, accident records,
highway traffic and roadside conditions not readily apparent to the driver."

The Engineering and Traffic Survey should contain sufficient information to document that the
conditions of CVC Section 627 have been complied with and that other conditions not readily
apparent to motorists are properly identified.

In determining the speed limit, which most appropriately facilitates the orderly movement of traffic
and is reasonable and prudent, crucial factors such as prevailing speeds, unexpected conditions,
and collision records are examined.

Determination of posted speed limits follow the latest CAMUTCD Policy as Revision 7 March 2023
by the State of California Department of Transportation. Speed limits shall be established at the
nearest 5 mph increment of the 85 th percentile speed of free-flowing traffic (CVC Section
22358.6(a)). However, in cases in which the speed limit needs to be rounded up to the nearest
five miles per hour increment of the 85th percentile speed, the Department of Transportation or a
local authority may decide to instead round down the speed limit to the lower five miles per hour
increment, but then the Department of Transportation or a local authority shall not reduce the
speed limit any further for any reason CVC 21400(4)(b).

An example of the application of this speed limit criteria is as follows:
  • If the 85th percentile speed in a speed survey is (37 MPH) then the speed limit would be
  posted at 35 MPH or optionally reduced to 30 MPH. However,
  • If the 85th percentile speed in a speed survey is (38 MPH) then the speed limit would be
  posted at 40 MPH or optionally reduced to 35 MPH.

The 85th percentile speed is often referred to as the critical speed. Pace speed is defined as the
10-mile increment of speed containing the largest number of vehicles. Speed limits established on
the basis of the 85th percentile conform to the consensus of those who drive highways as to what
speed is reasonable and prudent and are not dependent on the judgment of one or a few
individuals.

Basic speed law states that no person shall drive at a speed greater than is reasonable or prudent.
The majority of drivers comply with this law. Speed limits set at the 85 th percentile speed provide
law enforcement officers with a means of controlling drivers who will not conform to what the
majority considers reasonable and prudent.

The fundamentals used to establish speed limits recognize that the majority of drivers behave in a
safe and reasonable manner but need to be advised of conditions which may not be readily
apparent. For this reason, collision history, roadway conditions, traffic characteristics, and land
use, must be analyzed along with speed measurements to determine speed limits. Speed limit
changes are usually coordinated with visible changes in roadway conditions or roadside
developments.

In general, speed limits cannot be successfully enforced without voluntary compliance by a
majority of drivers. Consequently, only the driver whose behavior is clearly out of line with the
normal flow of traffic is considered a violator for enforcement purposes.

The radar equipment used to collect speed measurements was a SCOUT-MPH Traffic Radar, SHD-

The results of the radar speed measurements were computed, analyzed, and summarized on
standard Traffic Survey Forms. Significant values obtained from computations are as follows:

  •  The Critical Speed or 85th percentile speed, is the speed at or below which 85 percent of
  the traffic is moving. The Critical Speed is the primary guide in determining what the
  majority of drivers believe is safe and reasonable. Speed limits set higher than the Critical
  Speed are not considered reasonable and safe. The accepted practice is to set the speed
  limit at the nearest 5 MPH increment to the Critical Speed or 85th percentile speed unless
  other factors require a lower limit.

  •  The 5 or 10 MPH pace is a measure of the dispersion of speeds within the survey sample
  and is that 5 or 10 MPH increment containing the highest percentage of speeds in the total
  sample. The accepted practice is to keep the speed limit within the 10 MPH pace after
  considering the Critical Speed and any factors requiring a speed lower than the Critical
  Speed.

SECTION 3: SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS

The Engineering and Traffic Survey summaries presented in this report illustrate the results of a
thorough evaluation of the data collected and provides a recommended speed limit for each
street segment surveyed. In each case, the recommended speed limit is consistent with the
prevailing behavior as demonstrated by the radar speed measurements.

The Legislature, in adopting Section 22358.5 of the California Vehicle Code, has made it clear that
it is their intent that physical conditions such as width, curvature, grade and surface conditions, or
any other condition readily apparent to a driver, in the absence of other factors, would not require
special downward speed zoning. The basic rule of Section 22350 is sufficient regulation as to such
conditions.

The recommendations contained in this report were intended to establish prima facie speed limits.
Prima Facie limits advise the motorist and enforcement agencies of the reasonable speed for a
section of highway for prevailing conditions. They are not intended to be absolute. All violations
of these speed limits are violations of the basic speed law (Section 22350 of California Vehicle
Code). This statute states that a person shall not drive a vehicle as a speed greater than is safe
having regard for traffic, roadway, and weather conditions. A prima facie limit merely suggests a
safe speed under normal conditions.

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
 FROM:  Martha Garcia, Finance Director
 SUBJECT:  Adopt an Ordinance Establishing a Business License Tax Schedule

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Adopt an urgency ordinance establishing a business license tax schedule;
  2. Introduce and waive first reading of an ordinance establishing a business license
  tax schedule;
  3. Approve a one-time extension for renewal of business license tax, due and
  payable by April 1, 2025; and
  4. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
These actions are exempt from review under the California Environmental Quality Act
(California Public Resources Code §§ 2100, et seq., “CEQA”) and CEQA regulations (14
California Code of Regulations §§ 15000, et seq.) because they establish rules and
procedures to implement government funding mechanisms; do not involve any
commitment to a specific project which could result in a potentially significant physical
impact on the environment; and constitute an organizational or administrative activity that
will not result in direct or indirect physical changes in the environment. Accordingly,
neither of the propositions constitute a “project” that requires environmental review (see
specifically 14 CCR § 15378(b)(4-5)).

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
On November 5, 2024, voters adopted Measure BE which updated the structure of the
City’s business license tax to be based on a business’s gross receipts. The measure was
adopted based upon a 70.46% voter approval.

In order to continue to be an attractive place for larger businesses to operate, City staff is
recommending a scaled business license tax (BLT) schedule for businesses earning over
$25,000,000 annually. The City is also seeking approval for one-time extension for
renewal of business license tax, due and payable by April 1, 2025.

BACKGROUND:

  Page 384 of 431

December 18, 2024

Like many cities, the City of Monterey Park imposes a local business tax to help fund
municipal services within the community. The City uses these revenues for City services
such as police patrol, fire suppression, parks, recreation, maintenance services, library
services and senior programs. The business license tax is not regulatory; it is for revenue
generation only.

The Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) § 5.08.010 requires that any person (which
includes businesses) owning or transacting business in the City must obtain a license,
regardless of where the business is physically located.

Approximately seven of the current 4,700 businesses within the City are estimated to
gross over $25,000,000 in revenue annually. The next highest revenue grossing business
earns less than $10,000,000 annually. City staff is proposing to adopt a Resolution
allowing for a scaled BLT schedule that would ensure fairness while remaining business-
friendly to the seven extremely high grossing businesses. The Resolution permits an
automatic annual increase based on the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for All Urban
Consumers for the prior 12-month period ending on October 31st and would be applied
and effective on Janaury1st of each year (beginning January 1, 2026). Section 9 of
Measure BE authorizes the City Council to implement the BLT via regulations adopted by
ordinance.

To ensure that the City may collect the BLT on schedule, it is recommended that the City
adopt the draft urgency ordinance that would take effect immediately. This would allow
the City to begin collecting the BLT on January 1, 2025. Furthermore, Municipal Code §
5.08.210, states annual business license tax shall be due and payable in advance on the
first day of January of each year. To allow businesses to adjust to the new BLT structure,
the City is seeking approval for a one-time extension for renewal of business license tax,
due and payable by April 1, 2025.

2024-25 STRATEGIC PLAN GOAL:
With the passing of Measure BE, the City is seeking to achieve its goal of maintaining
fiscal stability of our City’s financial resources, specifically its objective of reviewing and
revising city revenue sources while also maintaining a business-friendly climate and
ensuring an equitable, fair, and modern business license tax base. Setting a BLT
Schedule will allow businesses grossing $25,000,000 or more annually to pay their fair
share without unduly impacting their overall operations and will help the City maintain
fiscal stability.

FISCAL IMPACT:
The City currently receives approximately $800,000 in BLT. The passing of Measure
BE inclusive of the business license tax schedule is expected to generate approximately
$1,200,000 annually for the city in general fund revenues, an increase of $400,000.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

The City conducted a review of the Employee Relations section in the Monterey Park
Municipal Code (“MPMC”). This occurred after the California Public Employment
Relations Board (“PERB”) found that the City’s procedures for recognizing
associations/unions were insufficient for making an appropriate union designation. The
proposed changes to MPMC Chapter 2.32 provide the appropriate procedures and
processes to recognize or appeal new associations/unions. City representatives
discussed and reviewed the MPMC section modification with representatives from the
current recognized associations/unions. The association/union representatives had an
opportunity to meet and discuss the impacts of the revisions and the groups agreed with
the revisions. The proposed amendments to the MPMC provide processes and
procedures for associations recognition along with appeal and decertification procedures.

California Environmental Quality Act (California Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et
seq., “CEQA”) and CEQA Guidelines (14 California Code of Regulations §§ 15000, et
seq.) pursuant to CEQA Guidelines § 15061(b)(3) because the Ordinance is for general
policies and procedure-making.

2.32.010 Purpose.
This chapter is authorized under Government Code Sections 3500, et seq., and is intended to provide
a means to promote full communication between the city and its employees to provide a reasonable
method of resolving disputes regarding wages, hours and other terms and conditions of employment.
The city must meet and confer in good faith regarding wages, hours, and other terms and conditions
of employment with representatives of recognized employee organizations and consider fully such
presentations as are made by the employee organization on behalf of its members before to arriving
at a determination of policy of course of action.

of recognition or during the 30 day period commencing 120 days before the termination date of a
Memorandum of Understanding then having been in effect less than three years, whichever
occurs later.

A Decertification Petition may be filed by two or more employees or their representative, or an

the duly authorized signatory under penalty of perjury under the laws of the state of California to
be true, correct, and complete:

1. The name, address and telephone number of the petitioner and a designated representative
  authorized to receive notices or requests for further information.

2. The name of the established appropriate unit and of the incumbent Recognized Employee
  Organization sought to be decertified as a representative of that unit.

3. An allegation that the incumbent recognized employee organization no longer represents a
  majority of the employees in the appropriate unit, and any other relevant and material facts
  relating thereto.

4. Proof of employee support that at least 30% of the employees in the established appropriate
  unit no longer desire to be represented by the incumbent Recognized Employee Organization.
  Such proof must be submitted for confirmation to the Employee Relations Officer within the
  time limits specified in this section.

An employee organization may, in satisfaction of the Decertification Petition requirements set forth
in this section, file a Petition under this Section in the form of a Recognition Petition that evidences

If the Employee Relations Officer determines the Petition is compliant, or if such a determination is
made following appeal, the Employee Relations Officer must give written notice of such

with names and all other identifying information redacted.

Thereafter, the Employee Relations Officer must arrange for a secret ballot election to be held on
or about 30 days after such notice to determine the wishes of unit employees as to the question of
decertification and, if a Recognition Petition was duly filed hereunder, the question of

 If, pursuant to this section, a different employee organization is formally acknowledged as the

2.32.070: Procedure for Modification of Established Appropriate Units.

A. Requests to modify established appropriate units must be submitted in the form of a petition for
  recognition and, in addition to the requirements, contain a complete statement of all relevant
  facts and citations in support of the proposed modified. The Employee Relations Officer shall
  process such petition as recognition petitions are processed.

B. When new classifications are adopted, existing classifications abolished, or when a
  classification is no longer compatible with the existing bargaining unit under the standards set
  forth in this chapter, the Employee Relations Officer may propose that an established unit be
  modified. The Employee Relations Officer must give written notice of the proposed
  modification(s) to any affected employee organization. Any affected employee organization,
  may, within seven days after service of notice, request a meeting with the Employee Relations
  Officer by which to contest the proposal(s). That meeting is informal and may consist of the
  participating employee organization providing verbal and/or written input regarding its position.
  Not later than seven days after receiving a request to meet, the Employee Relations Officer
  must conduct such meeting at which time all affected employee organizations must be heard.

  C. Thereafter, the Employee Relations Officer must determine the composition of the
  appropriate unit or units and give written notice of such determination to the affected
  employee organizations.

  D. The Employee Relations Officer determination may be appealed. If a unit is modified,
  employee organizations may thereafter file petitions of recognition seeking to become the
  recognized employee organization for such new appropriate unit(s).

2.32.080: Procedure for Processing Severance Requests.

An employee organization may file a request to become the recognized employee organization of
a unit alleged to be appropriate that consists of a group of employees who are already a part of a
larger established unit represented by another recognized employee organization. The timing,
form and processing of such request are as specified for modification requests.

2.32.090: Determination of Appropriate Unit.
A. The policy objectives in determining the appropriateness of units regarding the effect of a
  proposed unit are:

  1. Efficient operations of the city and its compatibility with the primary responsibility of the city
  and its employees to effectively and economically serve the public; and

  2. Providing employees with effective representation based on recognized community of
  interest considerations.
  Page 405 of 431
 B. These policy objectives require that the appropriate unit shall be the broadest feasible grouping
  of positions that share an identifiable community of interest. Factors to be considered are:

  1. Similarity of the general kinds of work performed, types of qualifications required, and the
  general working conditions.

  2. History of representation in the city and in similar employment; except however, that no unit
  may be deemed to be an appropriate unit solely on the basis of the extent to which
  employees in the proposed unit have organized.

  3. Consistency with the organizational patterns of the city.

  4. Number of employees and classifications, and the effect on the administration of employer-
  employee relations because of the fragmentation of classifications and/or proliferation of
  units.

  5. Effect on the classification structure and impact on the stability of the employer-employee
  relationship because of dividing a single or related classification among two or more units.

C. Notwithstanding the foregoing provisions, managerial, supervisory, and confidential
  responsibilities, are determinative factors in establishing appropriate units hereunder.
  Therefore, such managerial, supervisory, and confidential employees may not represent any
  employee organization which represents other employees and may only be included in a unit
  consisting solely of managerial, supervisory, or confidential employees respectively.

2.32.100: Appeals.

A. An employee organization aggrieved by a determination of the Employee Relations Officer that
  a Recognition Petition, Challenging Petition, Decertification Petition, Determination of an
  Appropriate Unit, Unit Modification Petition, or Severance Request was not filed in compliance
  with this chapter may, within 10 calendar days of notice thereof, appeal such determination to
  the City Manager for final decision.

B. Appeals to the City Manager must be filed in writing with the City Clerk and a copy be provided
  to the Employee Relations Officer by the appellant. The written appeal must be received by the
  City Clerk no later than 10 calendar days after the Employee Relations Officer sent a decision.
  An employee organization’s appeal must state the complete basis for the appeal and be
  confined to a determination of whether or not the unit resulting from the Employee Relations
  Officer’s decision was appropriate. The City Manager must issue a final written decision as to
  whether the Employee Relations Officer’s decision was appropriate. If the City Manager finds
  the decision was not appropriate, the City Manager will make the final decision.

C. The City Manager must conduct the appeal hearing within 15 calendar days after receiving the
  appeal and issue a written decision within 15 calendar days after conclusion of the hearing.
  The City Manager’s decision shall be final and binding. There is no right for an appeal to the
  city council.

 SUBJECT:  Emergency Replacement of the Fire Department Self-Contained
  Breathing Apparatus (SCBAs) – Adopt a Resolution authorizing the City
  Manager to execute necessary Agreements, without the need for
  competitive bidding to purchase the SCBA replacements

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Adopt a resolution ratifying the City Manager’s proclamation of local emergency
  dated December 11, 2024 concerning the replacement of Fire Department Self-
  Contained Breathing Apparatus (“SCBAs”) and authorizing the City Manager to
  execute necessary Agreements, without the need for competitive bidding to
  purchase the SCBA replacements;
  2. Appropriating $635,000 to the FY 2024-2025 Budget from the General Fund for
  the project; and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
Recently, the Fire Department Chief (“Chief”) was made aware that Honeywell, the sole
vendor who provides replacement parts and materials for the Fire Department’s
(“Department”) self-contained breathing apparatuses (“SCBA”), will no longer support
replacement parts and repairs as of December 16, 2024. By no longer supporting the
replacements parts and repairs, the Department’s current SCBAs will no longer be
approved by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (“NIOSH”) and can
no longer be used in occupational settings. Therefore, a local emergency exists and the
Department’s current SCBAs require immediate replacement.

The Chief recommends that the City Council adopt a resolution authorizing the City
Manager to execute necessary Agreements, without the need for competitive bidding for
the replacement of SCBAs for the Fire Department. This includes a quote for purchase
with Bauer Compressors for $633,812.92.

BACKGROUND:
Ordinarily, the City must comply with competitive bidding requirements of the Monterey
Park Municipal Code Chapter 3.20. However, due to the immediate need to address the
end of life of the existing SCBAs, competitive bidding for the proposed replacements
would be ineffective and impractical for the protection of fire suppression health and
safety.

As stated above, the SCBAs are critical personal protective equipment for fire
suppression personnel as they provide firefighters with breathable air while in dangerous
and toxic environments. SCBAs are imperative to the ability of fire suppression personnel
to do their jobs safely and appropriately.

The Chief obtained a quote from Bauer Compressors for 50 replacement SCBAs.
(Attachment No. 2). The quote includes the equipment, multi-year warranty, covering
maintenance and repairs, as well as training and support.

The Chief requests the City Council adopt a resolution authorizing the City Manager to
execute the necessary Agreements, in a form approved by the City Attorney, not to
exceed $635,000, with Bauer Compressors without the need for competitive bidding for
the emergency replacement of the Fire Department’s SCBAs. The Chief requests the
appropriation of $635,000 for costs associated with this project including the items and
service warranty.

2024-25 STRATEGIC PLAN GOAL:
The proposed Resolution supports the City’s strategic goal to maintain public safety with
a flexible and enhanced service model. The replacement of the expired SCBAs will
ensure that public safety is maintained.

FISCAL IMPACT:
Staff recommends the appropriation of $635,000 to the FY 2024-2025 Budget from the
General Fund to cover the costs of this purchase.

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider providing direction from the following
options:

  1. Authorizing the City Manager, or designee, to execute a license agreement, in a
  form approved by the City Attorney with the Monterey Park Woman’s Club to utilize
  the space within the Service Club House; or
  2. Taking no action, keeping the current facility reservation fees; and
  3. Taking such additional, related action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The Monterey Park Woman’s Club is an active 501 (c) 3 non-profit organization which
has provided community service to the residents of Monterey Park for over 100 years.
Their efforts support educational grants, domestic violence awareness, monetary support
programs, and partnerships with the Monterey Park Recreation & Community Services,
Bruggemeyer Library, and Fire and Police Departments.

The Monterey Park Woman’s Club meets once a month, from September through June,
in the Service Club House at Barnes Park. During the 2023/24 Fiscal Year, the Monterey
Park Woman’s Club paid $8.50 per hour based on the Fee Schedule for Non-Profit Adult
Organizations (Based in Town).

The City contracted with Wildan Financial Services to prepare a cost of service and fee
analysis for all city fees. On July 1, 2024, the City adopted the updated Master Fee
Schedule which includes the Non-Profit Adult (Based in Town) fee of $39.50 per hour.
The Monterey Park Woman’s Club has stated that the cost to reserve the Service Club
House facility for their monthly meetings presents a financial hardship.

Staff is recommending that City Council consider providing direction regarding the
reservation fees associated with the usage of the Service Club House by the Monterey
Park Woman’s Club.

BACKGROUND:
The Monterey Park Woman’s Club is a non-denominational, non-partisan, 501 (c) 3 non-
profit volunteer service organization. The club is a member of the General Federation of
Women’s Clubs International and the California Federation of Women’s Clubs. Their
members participate in a wide variety of service projects benefiting the Monterey Park
community.

The Monterey Park Woman’s Club has partnered with several City departments to
support community events, including the Monterey Park Community Services &
Recreation, Bruggemeyer Library, Fire and Police Departments. Regular events that the
Monterey Park Woman’s Club participate in are National Night Out and Monster Mash.
The club partners with the Lions Club to assist in recycling used eyeglasses.

Monterey Park Woman’s Club donates children’s books to the Bruggemeyer Library, Boys
& Girls Club of West San Gabriel Valley, YMCA, and Children’s Family Court. Their
monetary donations include supporting the Angeles National Forest through their Penny
Pines program and low-cost mammograms for breast cancer screening. During the
holiday season the club donates food items, toys and trees for local families in need. The
club also provides grants for local 7th grade girls to attend a camp at college campuses
focusing on STEM curriculum. In addition, the club provides domestic violence awareness
and prevention, along with support for victims and survivors.

FISCAL IMPACT:
The fiscal impact to City will vary based on City Council’s direction. The Woman’s Club
total fee for the 2023-2024 fiscal year was $255 for 30 hours at the $8.50 per hour Non-
Profit Adult (Based In Town) rate. Currently, the rate of a Non-Profit Adult (Based In Town)
is $39.50 per hour. If the Woman’s Club utilizes the Service Club House for 30 hours,
their total annual fee would be $1,185. If City Council decides to provide a license
agreement to the Woman’s Club, the fiscal impact would be a potential loss of revenue
of up to $1,185.
